case: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department at 2 AM because of a harsh, barking cough and noisy breathing that began a few hours earlier. For 2 days he has had rhinorrhea and a low-grade fever. Temperature is 38.1 °C (100.6 °F), pulse is 140/min, respirations are 40/min, and blood pressure is 96/60 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 95%. He is alert, sits comfortably on his mother's lap, and is not drooling. His voice is hoarse. Inspiratory stridor is heard at rest, with mild suprasternal retractions. An anteroposterior neck radiograph shows tapering narrowing of the subglottic trachea. Diagnosis: croup (viral laryngotracheobronchitis), most likely caused by parainfluenza virus.

questions.stem: He improves with treatment and is discharged. Four days later he returns with a temperature of 39.8 °C (103.6 °F), a toxic appearance, and worsening stridor that does not improve with nebulized epinephrine. He is not drooling. Laryngoscopy shows a normal epiglottis and thick purulent secretions in the trachea below the vocal folds. Which of the following organisms is most likely responsible for this new condition?
approach: High fever, a toxic look, and stridor that does not respond to epinephrine after a viral croup illness point away from simple croup.
A normal epiglottis rules out epiglottitis, and purulent secretions in the subglottic trachea define bacterial tracheitis.
Bacterial tracheitis is usually a secondary infection, most often by Staphylococcus aureus.
questions.why: Bacterial tracheitis is a bacterial superinfection of the trachea, often after a viral illness such as croup. The child becomes toxic, with high fever and thick pus in the trachea that can block the airway. Stridor does not improve with nebulized epinephrine, because the problem is pus and sloughed mucosa rather than mucosal edema alone. Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause. Simple croup, by contrast, causes a barking cough and stridor in a child who does not look toxic, and acute laryngitis in older children and adults causes hoarseness without stridor.
whyNot: Haemophilus influenzae type b causes epiglottitis, with drooling, tripod posture, and a swollen cherry-red epiglottis. This child's epiglottis is normal.
Respiratory syncytial virus causes bronchiolitis in infants, with wheezing and crackles, and does not cause toxic illness with purulent tracheal secretions.
Correct.
Bordetella pertussis causes paroxysmal coughing with an inspiratory whoop and lymphocytosis, not acute toxic stridor with tracheal pus.

topics: Croup versus bacterial tracheitis versus epiglottitis

questions.stem: Inspiratory stridor similar to this child's can occur in an adult after total thyroidectomy. Laryngoscopy shows both vocal folds fixed near the midline. Injury to which of the following nerves most likely explains these findings?
options: External branches of the superior laryngeal nerves
Internal branches of the superior laryngeal nerves
approach: Vocal folds stuck near the midline means the muscle that opens the glottis is not working.
The posterior cricoarytenoid is the only muscle that abducts the vocal folds.
It is supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve, so bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury causes stridor.
questions.why: The posterior cricoarytenoid muscle rotates the arytenoid cartilages so the vocal folds swing apart, and it is the only abductor of the folds. Like all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except the cricothyroid, it is supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve. Injury to one recurrent nerve causes hoarseness. Injury to both leaves the folds near the midline, so the airway is narrow and inspiratory stridor results. The left nerve loops under the aortic arch, so it can also be injured by aortic arch aneurysm or tumors in the aortopulmonary window.
whyNot: Correct.
The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve supplies the cricothyroid, which tenses the vocal folds. Injury causes a weak, low-pitched voice that tires easily, not stridor.

The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve carries sensation from the larynx above the vocal folds. Injury blunts the cough reflex and raises aspiration risk but does not fix the folds near the midline.
The glossopharyngeal nerve carries sensation from the oropharynx and supplies the stylopharyngeus. It has no motor role in the larynx.

topics: Intrinsic laryngeal muscles and their nerves

questions.stem: A nasal swab PCR assay detects parainfluenza virus type 1. This virus shares which of the following features with respiratory syncytial virus?
options: Positive-sense genome that acts as mRNA
approach: Parainfluenza virus is a paramyxovirus, and RSV is a pneumovirus that was formerly grouped with the paramyxoviruses.
Both are enveloped viruses with a nonsegmented, negative-sense RNA genome.
Both carry an F (fusion) protein that fuses infected cells into multinucleated syncytia.
questions.why: Parainfluenza virus and respiratory syncytial virus both have a nonsegmented, negative-sense RNA genome inside an envelope, and both use an F protein to fuse the viral envelope with the host cell membrane. F protein on infected cells also fuses neighboring cells into giant multinucleated syncytia, which gives RSV its name. Influenza differs by having a segmented genome with separate hemagglutinin and neuraminidase, and coronaviruses differ by having a positive-sense RNA genome.
whyNot: A segmented genome that can reassort belongs to influenza virus and allows antigenic shift. Parainfluenza and RSV genomes are not segmented.
A positive-sense RNA genome that can be translated directly belongs to coronaviruses and rhinoviruses. Parainfluenza and RSV carry negative-sense RNA and bring their own RNA polymerase.
Binding of the spike protein to ACE2 is the entry step of SARS-CoV-2, a coronavirus.
Correct.

questions.stem: As his work of breathing increases, he begins to contract his abdominal muscles forcefully during each expiration. Which of the following groups of brainstem neurons most directly drives this active expiration?
approach: Quiet expiration is passive and needs no expiratory muscles.
When ventilatory demand rises, expiratory muscles such as the abdominal wall muscles are recruited.
The ventral respiratory group in the medulla contains the expiratory neurons that drive forced breathing.
questions.why: In quiet breathing, the dorsal respiratory group in the medulla drives the inspiratory muscles, and expiration is passive recoil of the lungs and chest wall. When demand rises, as in this child with airway obstruction, the ventral respiratory group becomes active. It contains both inspiratory and expiratory neurons and drives accessory inspiratory muscles and the abdominal and internal intercostal muscles for forced expiration. The pontine centers fine-tune the timing of breaths rather than drive the expiratory muscles.
whyNot: The dorsal respiratory group, in the nucleus of the solitary tract, mainly drives inspiration and receives input from vagal and glossopharyngeal afferents. It is the main driver of quiet breathing.
Correct.
The pneumotaxic center in the upper pons limits the length of inspiration and so raises respiratory rate. It does not drive the expiratory muscles.
The apneustic center in the lower pons promotes prolonged inspiration. Damage below the pneumotaxic center with vagal loss gives apneustic breathing.

topics: Pontine respiratory centers and Hering-Breuer reflex

dx: Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease with nasal polyps and allergic rhinitis
case: A 41-year-old woman comes to the physician because of constant nasal congestion and loss of her sense of smell for 1 year. She developed asthma 3 years ago. On two occasions she had wheezing, worse nasal congestion, and facial flushing within 1 hour of taking ibuprofen. Each spring she has sneezing and itchy, watery eyes. Vital signs are within normal limits. The nasal mucosa is pale and boggy, and gray, glistening, soft masses fill both middle meatuses. Scattered expiratory wheezes are heard over both lungs. Blood eosinophil count is 850/μL (normal under 500). Diagnosis: aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease with bilateral nasal polyps and asthma, together with seasonal allergic rhinitis.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of chronic nasal obstruction. He has a chronic productive cough and poor weight gain with bulky, foul-smelling stools. Physical examination shows bilateral nasal polyps. Which of the following is the most likely underlying disorder?
approach: In adults, nasal polyps usually come with chronic rhinosinusitis, allergy, or aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease.
In a child, nasal polyps should prompt testing for cystic fibrosis.
Chronic productive cough plus fat malabsorption from pancreatic insufficiency completes the picture of cystic fibrosis.
questions.why: Nasal polyps are edematous outgrowths of inflamed sinonasal mucosa. In adults they come with chronic rhinosinusitis, allergy, and aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, and they cause nasal obstruction and loss of smell. In children they are unusual enough that cystic fibrosis should be suspected. Thick, dehydrated secretions block the sinuses and airways, and pancreatic duct blockage causes fat malabsorption with bulky, foul-smelling stools and poor weight gain.
whyNot: Correct.
Celiac disease causes malabsorption and poor growth but does not cause nasal polyps or a chronic productive cough.
Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency causes panacinar emphysema in adults and liver disease. It does not cause nasal polyps or pancreatic insufficiency.
Kartagener syndrome causes chronic sinusitis and bronchiectasis from immotile cilia, often with situs inversus, but the pancreas works normally, so fat malabsorption does not fit.

questions.stem: In November her husband develops sneezing, a scratchy throat, and clear rhinorrhea without fever. His nasal mucosa is red and swollen rather than pale. Which of the following properties of the most likely causative virus explains why it infects the nose but does not cause intestinal infection?
options: DNA genome replicated in the nucleus
approach: A common cold with red, swollen mucosa is infectious rhinitis, while her pale, boggy mucosa with eosinophilia reflects allergic rhinitis.
Rhinovirus is the main cause of the common cold.
Rhinovirus is a picornavirus that, unlike the enteroviruses in the same family, is destroyed by stomach acid.
questions.why: Rhinovirus causes most common colds. It is a small, nonenveloped, positive-sense RNA picornavirus that binds ICAM-1 on nasal epithelium. Unlike enteroviruses such as poliovirus, it is acid labile, so swallowed virus is destroyed in the stomach and it does not infect the gut. Infectious rhinitis gives red, swollen mucosa with neutrophils, while allergic rhinitis gives pale, boggy mucosa with IgE-driven mast cell release and eosinophils. Vasomotor rhinitis has neither infection nor allergy and is triggered by things such as cold air or odors.
whyNot: A segmented double-stranded RNA genome belongs to rotavirus, which infects the gut and causes diarrhea in young children.
Rhinovirus has no envelope. Enveloped viruses are generally destroyed by bile, but that is not the reason rhinovirus spares the gut.
Rhinovirus has an RNA genome that is replicated in the cytoplasm. DNA viruses such as adenovirus can cause both colds and gastrointestinal infection.
Correct.

topics: Allergic versus infectious versus vasomotor rhinitis

questions.stem: CT of the sinuses confirms that polyps fill both middle meatuses. Drainage from which of the following is most likely to be obstructed?
approach: The polyps sit in the middle meatus, below the middle concha.
The frontal, maxillary, and anterior ethmoid sinuses drain into the middle meatus.
Among the options, only the maxillary sinus drains there.
questions.why: The middle meatus receives the frontal sinus, the maxillary sinus through the semilunar hiatus, and the anterior ethmoidal cells. Polyps in this region therefore block these sinuses and cause chronic rhinosinusitis. The posterior ethmoidal cells drain into the superior meatus, the sphenoid sinus into the sphenoethmoidal recess, and the nasolacrimal duct into the inferior meatus.
whyNot: The sphenoid sinus drains into the sphenoethmoidal recess above the superior concha.
Correct.
The posterior ethmoidal cells drain into the superior meatus.
The nasolacrimal duct opens into the inferior meatus, below the inferior concha. Blockage there causes tearing (epiphora).

questions.stem: Her nasal and bronchial secretions are thick and tenacious. The main gel-forming component of this mucus is a family of large glycoproteins secreted by goblet cells and submucosal glands. Most of the carbohydrate chains on these proteins are attached to which of the following?
approach: The gel-forming glycoproteins of mucus are mucins.
Mucins are heavily O-glycosylated, with dense sugar chains along their protein backbone.
O-linked chains are attached to the hydroxyl group of serine or threonine in the Golgi apparatus.
questions.why: Mucins are long glycoproteins in which carbohydrate makes up most of the mass. The sugar chains start with N-acetylgalactosamine attached to the hydroxyl group of serine or threonine, an O-linkage added in the Golgi apparatus. These chains hold water and give mucus its gel properties. When goblet cells and submucosal glands enlarge, as in chronic bronchitis and chronic airway inflammation, more mucus is made. In cystic fibrosis the mucus is dehydrated, so it is too thick to clear.
whyNot: N-linked glycosylation attaches sugars to the amide nitrogen of asparagine and begins in the rough endoplasmic reticulum. It is common in membrane and secreted proteins but is not the main linkage in mucins.
Sugars attached to hydroxylysine are a feature of collagen, not of mucins.
Correct.
Lysine amino groups are sites of nonenzymatic glycation and of other modifications, such as ubiquitination, not of mucin carbohydrate chains.

topics: Airway mucus in chronic bronchitis and cystic fibrosis

dx: Acute bacterial maxillary sinusitis of odontogenic origin
case: A 52-year-old man comes to the physician because of 10 days of left cheek pain and pressure with foul-smelling, purulent discharge from the left nostril. A tooth in his left upper jaw had been painful for several weeks before the facial symptoms began. Temperature is 38.3 °C (100.9 °F), pulse is 92/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 134/82 mm Hg. There is tenderness over the left maxilla, and pus is seen draining from the left middle meatus. A carious upper left tooth is tender to percussion. CT shows an air-fluid level in the left maxillary sinus and a periapical lucency at the root of the diseased tooth, which projects into the sinus floor. Diagnosis: acute bacterial maxillary sinusitis of odontogenic origin.

questions.stem: Despite antibiotic treatment, 5 days later he has a temperature of 39.6 °C (103.3 °F), severe headache, and swelling of both eyelids. Both eyes are proptotic, he cannot abduct either eye, and sensation over his forehead is reduced on both sides. Which of the following is the most likely complication?
approach: Bilateral eye signs from a one-sided facial infection mean the infection has reached a midline structure that connects both sides.
Loss of abduction (cranial nerve VI) and reduced forehead sensation (V1) point to structures in or beside the cavernous sinus.
Infection reaches the cavernous sinus through valveless facial and ophthalmic veins, and the two cavernous sinuses connect across the midline.
questions.why: Cavernous sinus thrombosis is a septic clot in the cavernous sinus that follows infection of the face, sinuses, or teeth. Valveless facial and ophthalmic veins carry infection back to the sinus. Cranial nerves III, IV, V1, V2, and VI run through or beside the sinus, and VI is often affected first because it lies free in the sinus. Blocked orbital venous drainage causes proptosis and eyelid swelling, and spread through intercavernous connections makes the signs bilateral. Other sinusitis complications include orbital cellulitis, meningitis, brain abscess, and mucormycosis in diabetic ketoacidosis.
whyNot: Orbital cellulitis causes proptosis and painful eye movements on the side of the infected sinus, usually the ethmoid sinus. It does not explain signs in both eyes or loss of forehead sensation.
Correct.
Bacterial meningitis causes fever, headache, and neck stiffness, but not proptosis or eyelid swelling.
Rhinocerebral mucormycosis occurs mainly in diabetic ketoacidosis or severe immunosuppression and shows black necrotic tissue in the nose or palate. This patient has neither risk factor.

questions.stem: Which of the following teeth is most likely to be the source of his infection?
approach: Odontogenic sinusitis needs a tooth whose roots sit just under the floor of the maxillary sinus.
The roots of the maxillary molars, especially the first and second molars, lie closest to the sinus floor and may project into it.
Choose the maxillary first molar.
questions.why: The floor of the maxillary sinus sits over the roots of the upper molars and premolars. The roots of the first and second molars are closest and may project into the sinus with only a thin bony layer or mucosa between them. A periapical infection or an extraction of these teeth can therefore spread into the sinus. The maxillary sinus is also the sinus most often infected overall, because its ostium opens high on its medial wall, so gravity does not help it drain.
whyNot: The roots of the maxillary central incisor lie under the floor of the nasal cavity, far in front of the maxillary sinus.
The maxillary canine root lies in front of the maxillary sinus. Its infections usually spread into the soft tissues of the face (canine space) rather than through the sinus floor.
Correct.
Mandibular molar infections spread into the submandibular and sublingual spaces, as in Ludwig angina, not into the maxillary sinus.

questions.stem: Culture of a sinus aspirate grows anaerobes and alpha-hemolytic, gram-positive cocci. Which of the following test results would show that the cocci are the species that most often causes community-acquired pneumonia, rather than oral viridans streptococci?
approach: The most common cause of community-acquired pneumonia is Streptococcus pneumoniae.
Both S. pneumoniae and viridans streptococci are alpha-hemolytic, so a further test is needed to tell them apart.
S. pneumoniae is bile soluble and optochin sensitive, while viridans streptococci are bile insoluble and optochin resistant.
questions.why: Streptococcus pneumoniae is a lancet-shaped, gram-positive diplococcus that is alpha-hemolytic. Its autolysin is activated by bile salts, so colonies dissolve in bile, and it is inhibited by optochin. Viridans streptococci from the mouth are also alpha-hemolytic but resist both bile and optochin. S. pneumoniae is the most common cause of community-acquired and lobar pneumonia and a leading cause of bacterial sinusitis and otitis media. Its polysaccharide capsule is the main virulence factor, and it also makes IgA protease.
whyNot: Correct.
Growth in 6.5% sodium chloride identifies Enterococcus, which is usually gamma-hemolytic and rarely causes community-acquired pneumonia.
Resistance to optochin is the result expected for viridans streptococci. S. pneumoniae is optochin sensitive.
Bacitracin susceptibility identifies Streptococcus pyogenes, which is beta-hemolytic and causes pharyngitis.

questions.stem: Four months after dental treatment, his sinus symptoms persist. He now has crusting nasal ulcers, a cough with blood-streaked sputum, and red blood cell casts in his urine. Chest CT shows multiple cavitating nodules in both lungs. Which of the following serologic findings is most likely?
approach: Persistent sinus disease with nasal ulcers, cavitating lung nodules, and glomerulonephritis is the triad of granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis strongly linked to ANCA against proteinase 3.
Goodpasture syndrome also causes lung bleeding and glomerulonephritis but spares the upper airway and does not form cavitating nodules.
questions.why: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis causes necrotizing granulomas and vasculitis in the upper airway, lungs, and kidneys. Chronic sinusitis that does not resolve, nasal ulcers, and saddle nose deformity are typical upper airway signs. Lung nodules often cavitate, and the kidney lesion is a crescentic glomerulonephritis with red cell casts. Most patients have ANCA against proteinase 3, which gives a cytoplasmic (c-ANCA) staining pattern. Goodpasture syndrome, by contrast, is a type II hypersensitivity against the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen in glomerular and alveolar basement membranes.
whyNot: Anti-GBM antibodies against type IV collagen cause Goodpasture syndrome, with pulmonary hemorrhage and glomerulonephritis but no sinus disease or cavitating granulomas.
MPO-ANCA is typical of microscopic polyangiitis and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis. Microscopic polyangiitis lacks granulomas and upper airway disease.
Anti-dsDNA antibodies are specific for systemic lupus erythematosus, which can cause nephritis but not necrotizing granulomas of the sinuses and lungs.
Correct.

dx: Recurrent streptococcal tonsillopharyngitis with tonsillar hypertrophy and obstructive sleep apnea
case: A 6-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of 2 days of sore throat and fever. This is her seventh episode of sore throat in the past year. She has no cough or rhinorrhea. Her parents report loud snoring every night, pauses in her breathing followed by gasps, restless sleep, and poor attention at school. Temperature is 39.0 °C (102.2 °F), pulse is 118/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 98/62 mm Hg. Both palatine tonsils are red, covered with exudate, and so enlarged that they nearly touch in the midline. Tender anterior cervical lymph nodes are palpable. A rapid antigen test for group A streptococcus is positive. Diagnosis: recurrent streptococcal tonsillopharyngitis with tonsillar hypertrophy and obstructive sleep apnea.

questions.stem: Her 9-year-old brother, whose streptococcal pharyngitis last month was not treated, now has migratory polyarthritis and a new apical holosystolic murmur. Which of the following best explains the injury to his heart?
options: Direct invasion of the valve by streptococci
Immune complexes of streptococcal antigen in the valve
Antibodies to M protein that cross-react with heart
approach: Arthritis and a new mitral regurgitation murmur weeks after untreated streptococcal pharyngitis is acute rheumatic fever.
Rheumatic fever is an immune reaction, and no bacteria are found in the heart.
Antibodies and T cells made against streptococcal M protein cross-react with cardiac proteins such as myosin (molecular mimicry).
questions.why: Acute rheumatic fever follows Streptococcus pyogenes pharyngitis by about 2 to 4 weeks. The M protein of the bacterium resembles proteins in heart muscle and valves, so antibodies and T cells made against it also attack the heart. This is molecular mimicry, a type II hypersensitivity. The mitral valve is affected most often, giving mitral regurgitation acutely and mitral stenosis years later. Treating the pharyngitis with antibiotics prevents rheumatic fever, while poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis is an immune complex disease that antibiotics do not reliably prevent.
whyNot: Direct invasion of the valve describes infective endocarditis, in which blood cultures are positive and vegetations contain bacteria. Rheumatic valves are sterile.
Immune complex deposition is the mechanism of poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, which causes hematuria, edema, and hypertension, not valve disease.
Superantigens, such as streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins, cause streptococcal toxic shock syndrome and scarlet fever rash, not delayed valvulitis.
Correct.

questions.stem: She does not finish her antibiotic course. Four days later she has worsening throat pain on one side, difficulty opening her mouth, and a muffled voice. The uvula is deviated to the left. Which of the following is the most likely location of the abscess?
approach: One-sided throat pain, trismus, and a muffled voice after tonsillitis point to a peritonsillar abscess.
The abscess pushes the soft palate and uvula toward the opposite side.
A uvula deviated to the left means the abscess is on the right.
questions.why: A peritonsillar abscess forms between the tonsillar capsule and the superior constrictor muscle, usually as a complication of tonsillitis. The swelling bulges the soft palate on that side and pushes the uvula away from the abscess. Irritation of the nearby medial pterygoid muscle causes trismus, and the voice sounds muffled. Streptococcal tonsillitis should also be told apart from infectious mononucleosis, which gives exudative tonsillitis with posterior cervical nodes, atypical lymphocytes, a positive heterophile antibody test, and splenomegaly.
whyNot: A left-sided abscess would push the uvula to the right, away from the swelling.
Correct.
A retropharyngeal abscess causes neck stiffness, drooling, and bulging of the posterior pharyngeal wall, without uvular deviation. It occurs mostly in young children after nodal infection.
Infection of the sublingual and submandibular spaces (Ludwig angina) usually comes from a lower molar and causes firm swelling of the floor of the mouth that pushes the tongue up.

questions.stem: She also breathes through her mouth during the day, has a hyponasal voice, and has had three episodes of otitis media with effusion this year. Enlargement of which of the following best explains these additional findings?
approach: Hyponasal voice and mouth breathing mean the nasopharynx is blocked.
Recurrent middle ear effusions mean the pharyngotympanic tube opening, also in the nasopharynx, is blocked.
The lymphoid tissue in the roof and back wall of the nasopharynx is the pharyngeal tonsil (adenoids).
questions.why: Waldeyer ring is a ring of lymphoid tissue around the entrance to the pharynx: the pharyngeal tonsil (adenoids) in the nasopharynx, the tubal tonsils near the pharyngotympanic tube openings, the palatine tonsils in the oropharynx, and the lingual tonsil on the back of the tongue. Enlarged adenoids block airflow through the nose, so children breathe through the mouth, snore, and sound hyponasal. They also block the pharyngotympanic tube openings, so the middle ear cannot ventilate or drain, which leads to effusion and otitis media.
whyNot: The palatine tonsils lie in the oropharynx between the palatine arches. Their enlargement narrows the oropharynx and adds to her sleep apnea, but it does not block the pharyngotympanic tubes or the nasal airway.
The lingual tonsil lies on the posterior third of the tongue in the oropharynx, far from the pharyngotympanic tubes.
Correct.
The jugulodigastric node drains the palatine tonsil and enlarges with tonsillitis, but it lies in the neck and cannot block the airway or the pharyngotympanic tube.

questions.stem: Overnight polysomnography shows repeated episodes of absent airflow at the nose and mouth lasting 10 to 20 seconds, with continued and increasing chest and abdominal respiratory movements and falls in oxygen saturation. Which of the following best explains these events?
options: Collapse of the pharyngeal airway during sleep
Loss of brainstem respiratory drive during sleep
Diaphragm weakness from phrenic nerve injury
approach: Absent airflow with continued respiratory effort means the drive to breathe is intact but the airway is blocked.
This is obstructive sleep apnea, in which the pharynx collapses when muscle tone falls during sleep.
In this child, large tonsils and adenoids narrow the pharynx and make collapse more likely.
questions.why: In obstructive sleep apnea the pharyngeal airway collapses during sleep, when the dilator muscles relax. The brainstem keeps sending signals, so the chest and abdomen keep moving and effort increases until the patient briefly arouses and the airway reopens. In children, enlarged tonsils and adenoids are the most common cause, and removing them usually cures it. Repeated hypoxemia over years causes hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, which can lead to pulmonary hypertension, and can stimulate erythropoietin, causing secondary polycythemia.
whyNot: Correct.
Loss of brainstem drive is central sleep apnea. Airflow stops because chest and abdominal effort also stops.
Obesity hypoventilation syndrome is defined by daytime PaCO2 above 45 mm Hg with a BMI of 30 or more. It does not cause discrete apneas with rising effort, and this child is not described as obese.
Diaphragm weakness reduces effort, especially when lying down. It does not cause complete cessation of airflow while effort increases.

case: A 27-year-old woman comes to the physician because of shortness of breath that has worsened over 6 weeks. She has had night sweats and a 5-kg (11-lb) weight loss. Temperature is 37.2 °C (99.0 °F), pulse is 98/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. Breath sounds are absent and percussion is dull over the lower half of the left hemithorax. Chest CT shows a large anterior mediastinal mass and a left pleural effusion. Thoracentesis yields milky white fluid with a triglyceride concentration of 420 mg/dL (chylous if above 110). Biopsy of the mass shows Reed-Sternberg cells among bands of collagen and mixed inflammatory cells. Diagnosis: chylothorax from obstruction of the thoracic duct by nodular sclerosis Hodgkin lymphoma.

questions.stem: Lipoprotein analysis shows that the particles giving the pleural fluid its milky color are chylomicrons. These particles were assembled in which cells, and which lipid do they mainly carry?
approach: Chylous fluid is lymph from the intestine that has leaked out of the thoracic duct.
Intestinal lymph carries chylomicrons, made by enterocytes from absorbed dietary fat.
Chylomicrons are mostly triglyceride, which makes the fluid milky and gives a pleural triglyceride above 110 mg/dL.
questions.why: After a fatty meal, enterocytes repackage absorbed fatty acids and monoglycerides into triglyceride and load it onto apolipoprotein B-48 to form chylomicrons. These are too large to enter blood capillaries, so they enter intestinal lacteals and travel through the cisterna chyli and thoracic duct to the left venous angle. When the duct is torn or blocked, as by trauma, surgery, or lymphoma, this lymph leaks into the pleural space. The fluid is milky, has triglycerides above 110 mg/dL, and contains chylomicrons.
whyNot: Hepatocytes package endogenous triglyceride into VLDL, which enters the blood directly and is not carried in thoracic duct lymph in large amounts.
Particles rich in cholesteryl esters are LDL, which come from VLDL in the blood. Effusions rich in cholesterol (pseudochylothorax) form in old, long-standing effusions, not from duct obstruction.
Correct.
Adipocytes release free fatty acids bound to albumin and do not assemble lipoproteins.

questions.stem: The thoracic duct begins in the abdomen at the cisterna chyli. Which of the following describes where it passes through the diaphragm into the thorax?
options: Aortic hiatus, with the aorta and azygos vein
Esophageal hiatus, with the vagal trunks
Caval opening, with the right phrenic nerve
Sternocostal triangle, with the superior epigastric vessels
approach: The thoracic duct runs up behind the aorta and beside the azygos vein.
It leaves the abdomen with the aorta through the aortic hiatus at about T12.
It then rises in the posterior mediastinum, crosses to the left at about T5, and ends at the junction of the left subclavian and left internal jugular veins.
questions.why: The thoracic duct starts at the cisterna chyli near L1 to L2 and passes through the aortic hiatus at about T12 with the aorta and usually the azygos vein. It ascends in the posterior mediastinum between the aorta and azygos vein, crosses from right to left at about the level of T5, and empties into the venous angle where the left subclavian and left internal jugular veins join. Injury below about T5 tends to cause a right chylothorax, and injury above it a left chylothorax. A mediastinal lymphoma can compress or invade the duct anywhere along this path.
whyNot: Correct.
The esophageal hiatus at about T10 transmits the esophagus and the anterior and posterior vagal trunks.
The caval opening at about T8 transmits the inferior vena cava and branches of the right phrenic nerve.
The sternocostal triangle (foramen of Morgagni) transmits the superior epigastric vessels and is a site of anterior diaphragmatic hernia.

questions.stem: Additional studies show pleural fluid protein 4.0 g/dL, serum protein 6.5 g/dL, pleural fluid LDH 180 U/L, and serum LDH 210 U/L (upper limit of normal 220). Based on these results, the fluid falls into the same category as an effusion caused by which of the following?
approach: Apply Light criteria: an effusion is an exudate if any one criterion is met.
Protein ratio is 4.0/6.5, about 0.62 (above 0.5). LDH ratio is 180/210, about 0.86 (above 0.6). Pleural LDH is above two thirds of 220, which is about 147.
All three criteria are met, so the fluid is an exudate, like a parapneumonic effusion.
questions.why: Light criteria separate exudates, which come from inflammation, infection, or tumor that makes capillaries leaky or blocks lymph flow, from transudates, which come from changes in hydrostatic or oncotic pressure. An effusion is an exudate if the pleural to serum protein ratio is above 0.5, the pleural to serum LDH ratio is above 0.6, or the pleural LDH is above two thirds of the upper limit of normal for serum. This fluid meets all three. Bacterial pneumonia causes an exudative parapneumonic effusion, while heart failure, cirrhosis, and nephrotic syndrome cause transudates.
whyNot: Left ventricular failure raises capillary hydrostatic pressure and causes a transudate with low protein and LDH. It is the most common cause of pleural effusion.
Cirrhosis causes a transudate, from low albumin and from ascitic fluid moving through small diaphragmatic defects (hepatic hydrothorax).
Nephrotic syndrome causes a transudate because urinary protein loss lowers plasma oncotic pressure.
Correct.

questions.stem: She is treated with doxorubicin, bleomycin, vinblastine, and dacarbazine. Four months later she has a dry cough, exertional dyspnea, and fine bibasilar crackles. Pulmonary function tests show a restrictive pattern with a decreased diffusing capacity. Which of the following drugs most likely caused these findings?
approach: Dry cough, crackles, restriction, and a low diffusing capacity after chemotherapy suggest drug-induced pulmonary fibrosis.
Bleomycin is the classic chemotherapy drug that damages the lung.
Lung and skin have little bleomycin hydrolase, the enzyme that inactivates bleomycin.
questions.why: Bleomycin creates free radicals that break DNA. Most tissues inactivate it with bleomycin hydrolase, but the lungs and skin have little of this enzyme. Free radical injury damages pneumocytes and endothelium and leads to inflammation and then interstitial fibrosis, giving a restrictive pattern with a low diffusing capacity. Other drugs that cause pulmonary fibrosis include amiodarone, busulfan, and methotrexate. These must be ruled out before diagnosing idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.
whyNot: Doxorubicin is known for dose-dependent dilated cardiomyopathy, not pulmonary fibrosis.
Correct.
Vinblastine mainly causes bone marrow suppression, while its relative vincristine is known for peripheral neuropathy.
Dacarbazine is an alkylating agent that causes marked nausea and myelosuppression. It is not a classic cause of pulmonary fibrosis.

dx: Traumatic hemopneumothorax with flail chest after a motor vehicle collision
case: A 45-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after a high-speed motor vehicle collision in which he was the restrained driver. He has severe left chest pain and shortness of breath. Temperature is 36.6 °C (97.9 °F), pulse is 128/min, respirations are 32/min and shallow, and blood pressure is 88/54 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 87%. A segment of the left lateral chest wall moves inward during inspiration and outward during expiration. Breath sounds are decreased on the left. Chest radiograph shows fractures of the left fourth to seventh ribs, each broken in two places, and an air-fluid level in the left pleural space. Hemoglobin is 10.1 g/dL (normal 13.5 to 17.5). Diagnosis: left hemopneumothorax with flail chest.

questions.stem: A chest tube drains 1,100 mL of blood, and the bleeding stops. CT on day 5 shows about 500 mL of clotted blood that remains in the left pleural space. Without evacuation of this clot, which of the following is the most likely long-term consequence?
options: Bullous emphysema of the left lung
approach: Bloody pleural fluid with a hematocrit at least half the blood hematocrit is a hemothorax.
Retained clotted blood in the pleural space organizes, with fibroblasts laying down collagen.
The result is a thick fibrous peel over the visceral pleura that stops the lung from expanding (fibrothorax).
questions.why: A hemothorax is blood in the pleural space, defined by a pleural fluid hematocrit at least half the blood hematocrit. It usually follows chest trauma, and a large one causes hypovolemic shock as well as lung compression. Blood that is drained quickly causes little lasting harm. Retained clot organizes like any hematoma, and the fibrous peel it forms can encase the lung and fuse the pleural layers. This fibrothorax restricts lung expansion and may need surgical decortication. Retained blood can also become infected and form an empyema.
whyNot: Correct.
Chylothorax follows injury to the thoracic duct, which lies in the posterior mediastinum. Lateral rib fractures and blood in the pleural space do not cause it.
Malignant mesothelioma is linked to asbestos exposure decades earlier, not to retained blood.
Bullous emphysema results from destruction of alveolar walls, usually from smoking, and is not a consequence of a hemothorax.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why the injured chest wall segment moves inward during inspiration?
options: Greater elastic recoil of the injured lung
approach: Ribs broken in two places leave a segment that is no longer attached to the rest of the chest wall.
During inspiration, the diaphragm and intact chest wall expand the thorax, which makes pleural pressure more negative.
The free segment is sucked inward by this pressure instead of moving outward with the rest of the wall.
questions.why: Flail chest occurs when three or more adjacent ribs are each broken in two or more places, so a segment floats free of the chest wall. In inspiration, pleural pressure falls below its resting value of about minus 5 cm H2O, and the free segment is pulled in. In expiration, pleural pressure rises and the segment moves out. This paradoxical motion makes breathing less effective and painful. The more important cause of hypoxemia is often the underlying pulmonary contusion, which bleeds into alveoli and worsens over the first day.
whyNot: The internal intercostal muscles are expiratory muscles used in forced expiration. They do not explain inward movement during inspiration.
Lung elastic recoil pulls the lung inward all the time, but it does not change suddenly at each inspiration to move the segment.
Alveolar pressure falls below atmospheric during inspiration so air can flow in. It rises above atmospheric during expiration.
Correct.

topics: Pleural pressure during the breathing cycle

questions.stem: He is intubated and started on positive-pressure ventilation before the chest tube is placed. Minutes later his blood pressure falls to 70/40 mm Hg. His neck veins are distended, the trachea is deviated to the right, and the left chest is hyperresonant with absent breath sounds. Which of the following best explains his hypotension?
options: Loss of blood volume into the left pleural space
Impaired venous return from high intrathoracic pressure
Restricted ventricular filling from pericardial blood
Loss of sympathetic vascular tone from spinal cord injury
approach: Hyperresonance, absent breath sounds, tracheal deviation away from the affected side, and distended neck veins describe a tension pneumothorax.
Positive-pressure ventilation pushes more air through the lung injury into the pleural space, and a one-way valve traps it there.
The rising pressure compresses the great veins and shifts the mediastinum, so venous return and cardiac output fall.
questions.why: In a tension pneumothorax, air enters the pleural space with each breath but cannot leave. Pleural pressure rises above atmospheric, the lung collapses, and the mediastinum shifts to the opposite side. The high pressure compresses the venae cavae and the right heart, so venous return falls, neck veins distend, and blood pressure drops. Positive-pressure ventilation can quickly turn a simple traumatic pneumothorax into a tension pneumothorax. Needle decompression or a chest tube is lifesaving. Primary spontaneous pneumothorax occurs in tall, thin young men from ruptured apical blebs, and secondary pneumothorax occurs in lung diseases such as COPD.
whyNot: Blood loss into the chest causes hypotension with flat neck veins and dullness to percussion, not distended neck veins and hyperresonance.
Correct.
Cardiac tamponade also causes hypotension with distended neck veins, but breath sounds are present and the trachea stays midline.
Neurogenic shock from spinal cord injury causes hypotension with bradycardia and warm skin, and it does not cause tracheal deviation or one-sided hyperresonance.

questions.stem: To place the chest tube, the physician makes an incision in the left midaxillary line and passes the instrument through the fifth intercostal space just over the upper border of the sixth rib. This technique mainly protects which of the following?
options: Long thoracic nerve and lateral thoracic artery
approach: Each intercostal space has a neurovascular bundle that runs in the costal groove on the lower border of the rib above.
A needle or tube passed just over the upper border of the rib below stays away from this bundle.
The bundle is ordered from top to bottom as vein, artery, and nerve.
questions.why: The posterior intercostal vein, artery, and nerve run together in the costal groove along the inferior border of each rib, between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles. Entering the pleural space just above the upper border of a rib avoids injuring them. Chest tubes are placed in the midaxillary line at about the fourth or fifth intercostal space. In the midaxillary line the lower edge of the lung lies at about rib 8 and the pleura at about rib 10, so a needle placed too low can enter the costodiaphragmatic recess or pass through the diaphragm.
whyNot: The long thoracic nerve and lateral thoracic artery run on the surface of the serratus anterior. They can be injured by a cut that is too far posterior, but passing over a rib border does not protect them.
The internal thoracic vessels run vertically about 1 cm lateral to the sternum, far from a midaxillary approach.
Correct.
The thoracodorsal nerve and artery run along the posterior axillary wall to the latissimus dorsi, outside the intercostal space.

topics: Surface projections of the lungs and pleura

dx: Bronchial carcinoid tumor with obstructive atelectasis
case: A 38-year-old woman who has never smoked comes to the physician because of 4 months of cough, intermittent blood-streaked sputum, and wheezing on the right side of her chest. She has had two episodes of right-sided pneumonia in the past year. Vital signs are within normal limits. Breath sounds are decreased over the lower right chest, anteriorly and posteriorly. Bronchoscopy shows a smooth, red, polypoid mass that completely blocks the bronchus intermedius. Biopsy shows nests of uniform cells with round nuclei and finely stippled chromatin. Immunostaining is positive for chromogranin A and synaptophysin. Diagnosis: bronchial carcinoid tumor with obstructive atelectasis.

questions.stem: Which of the following additional histologic findings in the resected tumor is most consistent with this diagnosis?
approach: Chromogranin and synaptophysin show a neuroendocrine tumor, which could be a carcinoid or a small cell carcinoma.
A young never-smoker with a central polypoid mass and uniform cells fits a carcinoid tumor.
Carcinoid is low grade, so mitoses are rare and necrosis is absent.
questions.why: Bronchial carcinoid is a low-grade neuroendocrine tumor that arises from neuroendocrine (Kulchitsky) cells of the bronchial mucosa. It forms nests and cords of uniform cells with salt-and-pepper chromatin, few mitoses, and no necrosis in the typical form. It is not linked to smoking and often grows as a central polypoid mass that blocks a bronchus, causing cough, hemoptysis, and repeated pneumonia beyond the block. Because most tumors are small and make little serotonin, carcinoid syndrome is rare.
whyNot: Extensive necrosis with many mitoses describes small cell carcinoma, a high-grade neuroendocrine tumor seen almost only in smokers.
Correct.
Keratin pearls and intercellular bridges define squamous cell carcinoma, a central tumor strongly linked to smoking.
Lepidic growth along alveolar walls is the pattern of adenocarcinoma in situ, a peripheral tumor.

questions.stem: Which of the following chest radiograph findings is most likely?
options: Trachea shifted to the left with a flattened right hemidiaphragm
Trachea midline with air bronchograms in the right lower zone
Trachea shifted to the right with an elevated right hemidiaphragm
Trachea shifted to the left with a blunted right costophrenic angle
approach: A complete bronchial block traps air in the lobes beyond it.
Blood flowing past these alveoli absorbs the trapped gas, so the lobes collapse and lose volume.
Loss of volume pulls the trachea and mediastinum toward the collapse and raises the hemidiaphragm on that side.
questions.why: In obstructive (resorption) atelectasis, an airway is completely blocked by a tumor, mucus plug, or foreign body. Gas trapped in the alveoli beyond the block is gradually absorbed into the blood, so the lung tissue collapses. The volume loss pulls the mediastinum and trachea toward the affected side, raises the hemidiaphragm, and narrows the rib spaces. Compression atelectasis, from a large effusion or pneumothorax, does the opposite and pushes the mediastinum away.
whyNot: Shift away with a flattened hemidiaphragm is the picture of a large tension pneumothorax or hyperinflation on the right, not volume loss.
A midline trachea with air bronchograms describes consolidation, as in lobar pneumonia, in which the airways stay open and alveoli fill with fluid.
Correct.
Shift away with a blunted costophrenic angle describes a large pleural effusion that compresses the lung (compression atelectasis).

questions.stem: Which part of the right lung most likely remains ventilated?
options: Superior segment of the lower lobe
Medial basal segment of the lower lobe
approach: The right main bronchus gives off the upper lobe bronchus first.
The rest of the right main bronchus continues as the bronchus intermedius, which divides into the middle and lower lobe bronchi.
A block in the bronchus intermedius collapses the middle and lower lobes and spares the upper lobe.
questions.why: The right lung has three lobes separated by the horizontal and oblique fissures. The right upper lobe bronchus arises from the right main bronchus very close to the carina. The remaining airway, the bronchus intermedius, supplies the middle lobe and all segments of the lower lobe, including its superior segment. A mass in the bronchus intermedius therefore collapses both the middle and lower lobes. The left lung has two lobes, with the lingula of the upper lobe matching the right middle lobe. The right main bronchus is wider, shorter, and more vertical, so aspirated material usually lodges on the right.
whyNot: Correct.
The middle lobe bronchus arises from the bronchus intermedius, so the middle lobe collapses.
The superior segment of the lower lobe is supplied by a branch of the lower lobe bronchus beyond the bronchus intermedius. It is the usual site of aspiration in a supine patient.
The medial basal segment is supplied by the lower lobe bronchus beyond the block.

topics: Bronchial tree of the right lung

questions.stem: Arterial blood gas analysis on room air shows a PaO2 of 62 mm Hg (normal 75 to 100) and a PaCO2 of 37 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45). After 20 minutes of breathing 100% oxygen, the PaO2 rises only to 118 mm Hg. Which of the following best explains the poor response to oxygen?
options: Diffusion across the alveolar wall is slowed
Alveolar ventilation is low in all lung regions
Hemoglobin affinity for oxygen is decreased
Shunted blood never meets the added oxygen
approach: Collapsed lobes are still perfused but receive no ventilation, so their V/Q ratio is zero (shunt).
Blood passing through them leaves with mixed venous gas levels and mixes with blood from normal lung.
Extra inspired oxygen cannot reach shunted blood, and normal lung blood is already nearly saturated, so PaO2 rises little.
questions.why: A shunt is perfusion without ventilation, a V/Q of zero, as with a blocked airway or alveoli filled by pneumonia or edema. Blood from shunted areas stays deoxygenated, and because normal areas cannot carry much extra oxygen on already saturated hemoglobin, PaO2 stays low even on 100% oxygen. PaCO2 usually stays normal or low, because the respiratory drive raises ventilation of normal lung, which removes CO2 easily. Dead space is the opposite: ventilation without perfusion, a V/Q approaching infinity, as in pulmonary embolism, where wasted ventilation is the main problem.
whyNot: Slowed diffusion, as in interstitial fibrosis, causes hypoxemia that improves well with supplemental oxygen, because a higher alveolar PO2 drives more oxygen across.
Global hypoventilation raises PaCO2 and lowers PaO2, and both correct readily with oxygen. Her PaCO2 is normal.
Lower hemoglobin affinity for oxygen changes how oxygen is unloaded in tissues. It does not lower PaO2 or block the rise of PaO2 with oxygen.
Correct.

dx: High-altitude pulmonary edema in a climber
case: A 29-year-old man is brought to a high-altitude clinic at 4,500 m (about 14,800 ft) because of breathlessness at rest. He flew in from sea level and climbed to this altitude over 2 days. Over the past day he has had a dry cough that now produces pink, frothy sputum, and he cannot keep up with his group. Temperature is 37.8 °C (100.0 °F), pulse is 118/min, respirations are 30/min, and blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry shows an oxygen saturation of 68%. Crackles are heard over both mid lung fields. Chest radiograph shows patchy, asymmetric alveolar opacities with a normal heart size. Echocardiography shows high pulmonary artery pressure and normal left ventricular function. Diagnosis: high-altitude pulmonary edema.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the movement of fluid into his alveoli?
options: Raised left atrial pressure transmitted backward
Low plasma oncotic pressure from urinary protein loss
High flow through unconstricted capillary beds
Lymphatic obstruction by enlarged mediastinal nodes
approach: Normal left ventricular function and heart size make this a noncardiogenic edema, with a normal wedge pressure.
Alveolar hypoxia causes hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, which is patchy rather than even.
Blood is forced through the vessels that did not constrict, so capillary hydrostatic pressure there rises and fluid leaks out.
questions.why: Starling forces govern fluid movement across pulmonary capillaries: capillary hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid out, and plasma oncotic pressure holds it in. In cardiogenic edema, a high left atrial pressure (wedge pressure above about 18 mm Hg) raises capillary pressure everywhere. In high-altitude pulmonary edema, the left heart is normal, but hypoxic vasoconstriction is uneven. Unconstricted areas receive very high flow and pressure, and capillary walls leak and can break (stress failure). This gives patchy, asymmetric edema and high pulmonary artery pressure with a normal wedge pressure.
whyNot: Raised left atrial pressure causes cardiogenic edema, as in left heart failure or mitral stenosis. His left ventricle and heart size are normal.
Low oncotic pressure from protein loss occurs in nephrotic syndrome and causes generalized edema, not sudden lung edema on ascent.
Correct.
Lymphatic obstruction by tumor causes edema that develops slowly, and nothing suggests mediastinal disease in this healthy climber.

questions.stem: His climbing partner made the same ascent and feels well. Over the first several days at altitude, which of the following changes in the partner's kidney function best reflects normal acclimatization?
approach: Low inspired PO2 stimulates the peripheral chemoreceptors, so ventilation rises.
Hyperventilation lowers PaCO2 and causes a respiratory alkalosis.
Over days the kidneys compensate by excreting more bicarbonate, which lowers pH back toward normal.
questions.why: At high altitude, the low PaO2 stimulates the carotid bodies, so ventilation increases. This raises PaO2 but blows off CO2, causing respiratory alkalosis, which at first limits the rise in ventilation. Over several days, the kidneys excrete more bicarbonate, pH returns toward normal, and ventilation can rise further. Other parts of acclimatization include more erythropoietin and red cell mass, more red cell 2,3-BPG, and hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction. Acetazolamide speeds bicarbonate loss and is used to prevent acute mountain sickness.
whyNot: Correct.
Decreased bicarbonate excretion would worsen the alkalosis. It is the renal response to a respiratory acidosis.
Increased ammonium excretion is how the kidney excretes more acid, which is the response to acidosis, not alkalosis.
Increased titratable acid excretion also removes acid. It would make an alkalosis worse.

questions.stem: Within days, red cell 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG) rises in the partner, shifting the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve to the right. Which of the following inherited enzyme deficiencies also raises red cell 2,3-BPG through a direct effect on its synthetic pathway?
approach: 2,3-BPG is made in a side branch of red cell glycolysis from 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate (the Rapoport-Luebering shunt).
A block below this branch point causes the intermediates above it to build up, so more 2,3-BPG forms.
Pyruvate kinase catalyzes the last step of glycolysis, so its deficiency raises 2,3-BPG.
questions.why: In red cells, bisphosphoglycerate mutase converts some 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate to 2,3-BPG. 2,3-BPG binds deoxyhemoglobin and stabilizes the T (tense) form, so hemoglobin gives up oxygen more easily in tissues. Hypoxia at altitude raises 2,3-BPG. In pyruvate kinase deficiency, glycolytic intermediates back up behind the block, more 2,3-BPG is made, and the curve shifts right, so patients tolerate their anemia relatively well. A block above the branch point, such as hexokinase deficiency, has the opposite effect.
whyNot: G6PD deficiency affects the pentose phosphate pathway and NADPH production. It causes hemolysis under oxidant stress but does not directly raise 2,3-BPG.
Hexokinase acts at the first step of glycolysis, above the 2,3-BPG branch point. Its deficiency lowers 2,3-BPG and shifts the curve to the left.
Correct.
Cytochrome b5 reductase deficiency causes methemoglobinemia, which shifts the curve to the left. It does not raise 2,3-BPG.

questions.stem: At the clinic, his hemoglobin concentration is 15.0 g/dL (normal 13.5 to 17.5), arterial oxygen saturation is 68%, and PaO2 is 36 mm Hg. Which of the following is closest to his arterial oxygen content, in mL O2/dL of blood?
approach: Oxygen content equals bound oxygen (1.34 x Hb x SaO2) plus dissolved oxygen (0.003 x PaO2).
Bound oxygen: 1.34 x 15.0 x 0.68 is about 13.7 mL/dL. Dissolved oxygen: 0.003 x 36 is about 0.1 mL/dL.
The total is about 13.8 mL/dL.
questions.why: Almost all oxygen in blood is carried on hemoglobin, with each gram binding about 1.34 mL of O2 when fully saturated. Dissolved oxygen adds only 0.003 mL/dL per mm Hg of PaO2. With a normal hemoglobin but a saturation of 68%, his oxygen content is about 13.8 mL/dL, far below the normal of about 20 mL/dL. Anemia lowers content with a normal PaO2 and SaO2. Polycythemia raises content. Carbon monoxide lowers SaO2 and content while PaO2 stays normal.
whyNot: 10.3 results from using 1.0 instead of 1.34 mL O2 per gram of hemoglobin.
Correct.
14.7 results from multiplying PaO2 by 0.03 instead of 0.003, which overstates the dissolved oxygen tenfold.
20.2 is the content if hemoglobin were fully saturated, which is about normal at sea level.

topics: Effects of anemia and carbon monoxide on oxygen content

dx: Pulmonary embolism with pulmonary infarction after hip surgery
case: A 72-year-old woman develops sudden shortness of breath and right-sided chest pain that worsens with inspiration 6 days after surgical repair of a femoral neck fracture. She has coughed up small amounts of blood. She has chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. Temperature is 37.9 °C (100.2 °F), pulse is 112/min, respirations are 26/min, and blood pressure is 132/80 mm Hg. Her left calf is swollen and tender. Arterial blood gas analysis on room air shows pH 7.48 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), PaCO2 31 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45), and PaO2 62 mm Hg (normal 75 to 100). D-dimer concentration is increased. CT pulmonary angiography shows filling defects in segmental arteries of the right lower lobe and a peripheral, wedge-shaped opacity that touches the pleura. Diagnosis: pulmonary embolism with pulmonary infarction.

questions.stem: She is breathing room air at sea level (inspired oxygen fraction 0.21, barometric pressure 760 mm Hg, water vapor pressure 47 mm Hg). Assuming a respiratory quotient of 0.8, which of the following is closest to her alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient?
approach: Alveolar PO2 = 0.21 x (760 minus 47) minus PaCO2/0.8 = 149.7 minus 38.8, which is about 111 mm Hg.
A-a gradient = alveolar PO2 minus PaO2 = 111 minus 62, which is about 49 mm Hg.
A normal gradient at her age is about 20 to 25 mm Hg, so this gradient is widened.
questions.why: The alveolar gas equation gives alveolar PO2 from inspired oxygen and PaCO2. Her alveolar PO2 is about 111 mm Hg, so the A-a gradient is about 49 mm Hg, well above normal. Pulmonary embolism widens the gradient because blood is diverted to unblocked vessels, creating areas of low V/Q, and atelectasis adds some shunt. Hyperventilation from hypoxemia and receptor stimulation lowers PaCO2 and causes respiratory alkalosis. Most emboli start as deep vein thrombi in the legs, formed under the conditions of Virchow triad: stasis, endothelial injury, and hypercoagulability, all present after hip surgery.
whyNot: 12 mm Hg is within the normal range, as seen when hypoxemia comes only from hypoventilation or low inspired oxygen. It does not fit a PE.
Correct.
88 mm Hg results from leaving out the PaCO2/0.8 term (149.7 minus 62).
111 mm Hg is the alveolar PO2 itself, before PaO2 is subtracted.

topics: Alveolar gas equation and A-a gradient

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the gross appearance of the lung lesion seen as the peripheral opacity?
options: Pale wedge with its base on the pleura
Red wedge with its apex on the pleura
Pale cavity with a liquefied center
Red wedge with its base on the pleura
approach: A blocked artery supplies a cone of tissue that widens toward the periphery, so the infarct is wedge-shaped with its base at the pleura.
The lung has a dual blood supply and loose tissue, so blood from bronchial arteries leaks into the dead area.
Lung infarcts are therefore red (hemorrhagic).
questions.why: Pulmonary infarcts are wedge-shaped, with the apex pointing to the blocked vessel and the base on the pleural surface. They are hemorrhagic because bronchial arterial blood continues to flow into the necrotic area and the loose lung tissue lets blood collect. Infarction follows blockage of a medium or small artery, usually when bronchial flow is also reduced, as in heart failure. Hemoptysis comes from bleeding into the alveoli, and pleuritic pain comes from inflammation of the overlying pleura, often with a fibrinous exudate.
whyNot: Pale (anemic) infarcts occur in solid organs with end-arterial blood supply, such as the heart, kidney, and spleen.
The apex of the wedge points toward the blocked artery near the hilum, not toward the pleura.
A cavity with a liquefied center describes a lung abscess or a septic infarct, not a bland embolic infarct.
Correct.

questions.stem: Most pulmonary emboli in people with normal cardiac function do not cause infarction. Which of the following best explains this?
options: Bronchial arteries keep supplying the lung tissue
Pulmonary veins refill the segment in reverse
Hypoxic vasoconstriction diverts flow to the segment
Fibrinolysis clears every embolus within minutes
approach: The lung has two blood supplies: the pulmonary arteries for gas exchange and the bronchial arteries for the lung tissue itself.
Bronchial arteries arise from the systemic circulation, mostly from the aorta, and continue to perfuse tissue beyond a pulmonary embolus.
Infarction happens mainly when bronchial flow is also poor, as in her heart failure.
questions.why: The pulmonary circulation carries the whole cardiac output at low pressure (mean about 15 mm Hg) and low resistance, for gas exchange. The bronchial arteries are small systemic vessels from the aorta that nourish the bronchi and supporting tissue, and they connect with the pulmonary circulation. When a pulmonary artery is blocked, bronchial blood keeps the tissue alive, so fewer than about 10% of emboli cause infarction. In heart failure, low cardiac output and lung congestion reduce this backup flow, so infarction is more likely.
whyNot: Correct.
Pulmonary veins carry blood away from the alveoli toward the left atrium. They do not reverse flow to rescue a blocked segment.
Hypoxic vasoconstriction diverts blood away from poorly ventilated alveoli, not toward an area whose artery is blocked.
Fibrinolysis does break down emboli, but over days to weeks, not within minutes, and it does not explain why most emboli spare the tissue.

questions.stem: On the same ward, a 22-year-old man with a femoral shaft fracture from a motorcycle crash becomes confused and short of breath 36 hours after the injury. He has petechiae over the upper chest, axillae, and conjunctivae. Which of the following is the most likely source of the embolic material?
options: Thrombus from deep veins of the calf
Air entering a central venous catheter
Fat globules from injured bone marrow
approach: A long bone fracture followed in 1 to 3 days by hypoxemia, confusion, and petechiae is the triad of fat embolism syndrome.
Marrow fat enters torn veins at the fracture site and lodges in the lung capillaries.
Fat droplets and their breakdown products also reach the brain and skin, causing confusion and petechiae.
questions.why: Fat embolism syndrome follows long bone or pelvic fractures, usually 24 to 72 hours after injury. Marrow fat globules enter torn venules, block lung capillaries, and are broken down to free fatty acids that injure the endothelium. Some globules pass into the systemic circulation and block small vessels in the brain and skin, causing confusion and petechiae, typically on the upper body, axillae, and conjunctivae. Air embolism follows central line handling or rapid ascent in divers, and amniotic fluid embolism causes sudden collapse and DIC during delivery.
whyNot: A thromboembolus from the calf causes dyspnea and hypoxemia, but it does not cause petechiae and does not explain confusion in this young man.
Air embolism occurs suddenly when air enters an open central line or during decompression in divers. There is no catheter event here.
Correct.
Septic emboli from tricuspid endocarditis, as in injection drug use, cause multiple cavitating lung nodules with fever and a murmur.

dx: Lung adenocarcinoma with an EGFR mutation in a never-smoker
case: A 49-year-old woman who has never smoked comes to the physician because of a dry cough for 3 months and a 4-kg (9-lb) weight loss. Vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Chest CT shows a 3.2-cm peripheral nodule with irregular, spiculated margins in the left upper lobe. CT-guided biopsy shows gland-forming tumor cells with intracellular mucin that stain positive for thyroid transcription factor 1 (TTF-1). Molecular testing of the tumor shows an exon 19 deletion in the EGFR gene. Diagnosis: lung adenocarcinoma with an EGFR mutation.

questions.stem: The resected lobe also contains a separate 1.0-cm nodule. In this nodule, tumor cells grow along intact alveolar walls, with no invasion of the stroma, blood vessels, or pleura. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis of this second nodule?
approach: Growth of tumor cells along intact alveolar walls is called lepidic growth.
A small lesion with only lepidic growth and no invasion is adenocarcinoma in situ.
Any invasion of stroma, vessels, or pleura would make it an invasive adenocarcinoma.
questions.why: Adenocarcinoma is the most common lung cancer overall and the most common in never-smokers and women. It is usually peripheral and forms glands or makes mucin. Adenocarcinoma in situ is a small lesion, 3 cm or less, in which tumor cells spread along the alveolar walls (lepidic growth) without invading. It was formerly called bronchioloalveolar carcinoma. Complete resection of adenocarcinoma in situ is curative.
whyNot: Invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma has tall mucin-filled cells that invade tissue and often spread through the airways to many sites.
Squamous cell carcinoma in situ arises in central bronchial epithelium after squamous metaplasia and dysplasia, usually in smokers, not along alveolar walls.
Large cell carcinoma is an invasive, poorly differentiated tumor with large cells and no gland or squamous differentiation.
Correct.

topics: Adenocarcinoma in situ and lepidic growth

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the effect of this mutation on the encoded protein?
options: Lost GTPase activity in a membrane-bound G protein
Gene fusion creating a constitutively active ALK kinase
Loss of a nuclear protein that halts the cell cycle
approach: EGFR encodes the epidermal growth factor receptor, a transmembrane receptor tyrosine kinase.
Exon 19 deletions in its kinase domain are gain-of-function mutations.
The receptor signals without its ligand, driving growth through pathways such as RAS-MAPK and PI3K-AKT.
questions.why: EGFR is a receptor tyrosine kinase that normally signals only after epidermal growth factor binds and two receptors pair up. Exon 19 deletions and the L858R point mutation activate the kinase domain so it signals all the time. These mutations are most common in adenocarcinomas of never-smokers, women, and people of East Asian ancestry. Tumors with them often respond to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors. Other adenocarcinoma drivers are KRAS mutations (more common in smokers) and ALK rearrangements, while small cell carcinoma nearly always has TP53 and RB1 loss.
whyNot: Correct.
Loss of GTPase activity describes activating KRAS mutations, which keep RAS in its GTP-bound active state. KRAS mutations occur mainly in smokers.
ALK rearrangements, such as EML4-ALK, are gene fusions that also activate a kinase, but they are a different alteration from an EGFR exon 19 deletion.
Loss of a nuclear brake on the cell cycle describes tumor suppressors such as RB1 and TP53, which are lost in small cell carcinoma.

questions.stem: Before biopsy, the differential diagnosis for the nodule included a benign hamartoma. Which of the following CT findings would most strongly have favored hamartoma?
options: Multiple round nodules in both lungs
Thick-walled cavity with an air-fluid level
approach: A pulmonary hamartoma is a benign nodule made of mature cartilage, fat, and connective tissue.
Calcified cartilage gives a popcorn pattern on imaging, and fat gives low density.
These two features together strongly favor a hamartoma over a malignancy.
questions.why: Pulmonary hamartoma is the most common benign lung tumor. It is a well-circumscribed nodule of disorganized mature cartilage, fat, and connective tissue, usually found by chance in adults. Popcorn-like calcification from the cartilage and fat within the nodule are its classic CT signs. Metastases are more common than primary lung cancer and usually appear as several round, well-circumscribed nodules in both lungs. Spiculated margins favor a primary lung cancer, as in this patient.
whyNot: Spiculated margins and pleural retraction suggest an infiltrating primary lung cancer, as in this patient.
Multiple round, well-circumscribed nodules in both lungs are typical of metastases, which reach the lung by the blood.
Correct.
A thick-walled cavity suggests squamous cell carcinoma, lung abscess, or tuberculosis, not a hamartoma.

questions.stem: Electron microscopy of some tumor cells shows cytoplasmic lamellar bodies, a feature of one type of normal alveolar lining cell. In addition to secreting surfactant, that normal cell does which of the following?
options: Forms most of the alveolar gas-exchange surface
Regenerates type I cells after alveolar injury
Phagocytoses inhaled particles in the alveoli
Moves mucus toward the pharynx with its cilia
approach: Lamellar bodies store surfactant and are found in type II pneumocytes.
Type II pneumocytes are also the stem cells of the alveolar lining.
After injury they divide and replace type I pneumocytes.
questions.why: Type II pneumocytes are cuboidal cells that make up a small share of the alveolar surface. They make surfactant, stored in lamellar bodies, which lowers surface tension and keeps alveoli open. They also divide after alveolar injury and differentiate into type I pneumocytes, so type II cell hyperplasia is a sign of repair. Type I pneumocytes are thin, flat cells that cover most of the alveolar surface for gas exchange. Club cells in the bronchioles secrete protective proteins, detoxify inhaled compounds with cytochrome P450, and act as local progenitors.
whyNot: Type I pneumocytes are thin, flat cells that form about 95% of the alveolar surface and the gas-exchange barrier. They do not make surfactant.
Correct.
Alveolar macrophages phagocytose inhaled particles and microbes. They come from blood monocytes and do not make surfactant.
Ciliated columnar cells move mucus up the airways, but they line the bronchi and bronchioles, not the alveoli.
